solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Backers singing about god in Luxor

blocks.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
Horus is the falcon-headed Egyptian god

explanation.surface: A backing group sings a hymn about a deity in the Egyptian city of Luxor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Luxor' is not a container instruction; it just tells you the god is an Egyptian one.
explanation.definitionFit: A chorus is the group of singers who back up the soloist or principal performers.

clue.text: Those struggling to grasp university having work stack up here?

indicators.note: something struggling is thrashing about, so its letters are thrown out of order
to grasp something is to hold it, so one piece closes round another

blocks.note: the letters of 'those' rearranged
U is the standard abbreviation for university
OP, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: People struggling with a university workload find the work piling up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stack' is not a pile of work but a chimney stack, and the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Chimney stacks rise from the roof, so the top of a house is where you would find one.

clue.text: Served up beer no-one’s consumed within district

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase, matching the adjective

indicators.note: in a down clue, something served up is brought upward, so it reads bottom to top
what is consumed goes inside the consumer, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: lager is a type of beer
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone drank a beer that nobody else had touched in the local area.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated 'no-one' is not a single word here: it breaks into two pieces, and the reversal applies to the whole assembly, not just the beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something regional belongs to or happens inside a particular area or part of a country.

clue.text: Dubious citizen turning up in peculiar places

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up makes the letters read from the bottom upward
peculiar means strange or out of the ordinary, so the letters take an odd new order
one piece sits in another, placed within it

blocks.note: CIT is an old shortening of citizen
the letters of 'places' rearranged

explanation.surface: A shady resident keeps appearing in strange locations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dubious' reads as a description of the citizen but is the definition; the reversed citizen sits inside the rearranged places.
explanation.definitionFit: Being dubious about a claim means doubting it, the attitude of someone inclined to disbelieve.

clue.text: Vital bit of gear arrived shortly before opening of mine

indicators.note: said shortly, a word is cut short, losing its final letter

blocks.note: CAME, meaning arrived, minus its last letter
a mine is entered by a vertical shaft

explanation.surface: An essential piece of mining equipment turned up just before the pit opened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening of mine' looks like it wants the letter M, but here it is a whole word for the way into a mine.
explanation.definitionFit: In an engine the rotating shaft with cams drives the valves, an essential part of the gearing.

clue.text: Possibly failure to affirm / what corrupt tennis player should earn?

definitions.text: what corrupt tennis player should earn?

blocks.note: first meaning: refusing to swear or affirm in the witness box is one example of this legal offence

blocks.clueFragment: what corrupt tennis player should earn?
blocks.note: second meaning, read whimsically: scorn for someone who cheats on the tennis court

explanation.walkthrough: To affirm is to make a solemn non-religious promise in court instead of an oath, so declining is an offence. The second half puns on the tennis court.
explanation.definitionFit: Disobeying or disrespecting a judge's authority is a legal offence, and a match-fixer deserves disdain on the playing surface.

clue.text: Squiffy contestants finally given ratings

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of a word, so only its last letter is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
ratings are ordinary sailors, so a ship given them is crewed

explanation.surface: Tipsy competitors at last receive their scores from the judges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ratings' looks like scores on a talent show; in crosswords ratings are naval seamen, so the ship is crewed.
explanation.definitionFit: Squiffy and screwed are both informal British slang for drunk, a mild intoxication.

clue.text: Take good notice of / nurse

blocks.note: first meaning: pay close heed to
second meaning: look after someone who is ill

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurse' reads as a noun after the first phrase, but it is a verb, matching the phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to pay careful heed to something and to care for a sick patient.

clue.text: Particular period allocated by fate

blocks.note: in arithmetic, three by four is three times four
your lot is your fate in life

explanation.surface: A certain stretch of time was handed out by destiny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Allocated by fate' reads as one phrase, but 'allocated' belongs to the definition and 'by' is the multiplication sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A slot is an assigned window in a schedule, such as a broadcast or appointment booked for someone.

clue.text: Chap has mistakenly begun to restrict pulse

indicators.note: done mistakenly means done wrongly, so the letters come out in the wrong order
to restrict is to hem in, so one piece is enclosed by the other

blocks.note: a chap is a man
the letters of 'begun' rearranged

explanation.surface: A man wrongly started trying to limit his heart rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' suggests a heartbeat, but it is the edible seed of a legume. The rearranged letters sit inside M-AN.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulses are dried edible seeds of leguminous plants, and this small green bean is one example.

clue.text: Master satisfied to retire for the present

indicators.note: to retire is to withdraw or go back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a pro, or professional, is a master of a skill
a need that is satisfied has been met

explanation.surface: A contented schoolmaster is happy to stop working for now.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is short for Latin pro tempore; 'retire' sounds like the master's career plan but only flips the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin tag means for the time being, used of temporary arrangements or acting officeholders.

clue.text: Left in river beginning to expire, he’s put out

indicators.note: one piece is placed in another, inside it
the beginning of a word is its opening letter, which is all that is kept

blocks.note: the Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland
port is the left side of a ship
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A man left in a river on the point of dying is thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' is a jokey way to describe someone expelled from a country; 'Left' is the ship's side, not departed.
explanation.definitionFit: A deportee is a person expelled from a country by the state, literally put out of it.

clue.text: Shows off pens, perhaps 1000 collected

indicators.note: things collected are gathered in, so one piece is taken inside another

blocks.note: a pen is a female swan; 'perhaps' marks it as an example
K stands for a thousand, from kilo

explanation.surface: Someone flaunts a collection of a thousand fountain pens.
explanation.walkthrough: The writing pens are a false scent: a pen is a female swan.
explanation.definitionFit: To swank is British informal for behaving boastfully, parading wealth or talents to impress.

clue.text: Standard / bore

blocks.note: first meaning: generally agreed or conventional
second meaning: put up with, the past tense of bear

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like a tedious person or a drilled hole; here it is the past tense of bear, meaning tolerated.
explanation.definitionFit: The word works as an adjective for what is conventionally recognised and as a verb for having tolerated something.

clue.text: Slap person tailing gumshoe?

blocks.note: a gumshoe is a private detective, a private eye
someone who tails a person shadows them; tailing also puts this piece after the other

explanation.surface: A detective's quarry slaps whoever is following him.
explanation.walkthrough: Slap is British slang for make-up, not a blow. The follower comes after the detective, so EYE leads.
explanation.definitionFit: Slap is informal British for cosmetics, and coloured powder for the eyelids is one kind of make-up.

clue.text: Receding flow of water over stone

indicators.note: something receding goes backwards, so the letters are read from the end

blocks.note: water laps against a shore
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A retreating tide washes over a pebble on the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' reads as a preposition but supplies the letter; LAP plus O is turned round whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Opal is an iridescent gemstone, so it is a precious stone used in jewellery.

clue.text: Hindrance alumni deal with, not Keble’s first

indicators.note: not tells you to leave something out of the word it follows
first picks out the opening letter of a word and nothing more

blocks.note: former pupils are old boys, OBs
to deal with a problem is to tackle it
the opening letter of the college name, the letter taken out

explanation.surface: Former students have a problem to handle that doesn't involve an Oxford college.
explanation.walkthrough: K comes out of TACKLE. Keble is an Oxford college, which makes 'alumni' feel natural in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An obstacle is something that blocks progress, the same idea as a hindrance or impediment.

clue.text: Against endless search for survivors from the past

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: anti means against
QUEST, a search, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone opposes a never-ending hunt for people who lived through a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Survivors' suggests people rescued from a disaster; here they are old objects that have lasted.
explanation.definitionFit: Antiques are old collectable objects, things that have lasted from earlier generations into today.

clue.text: Egyptian believer collared when speaking

indicators.note: when speaking means the word is judged by its pronunciation rather than its spelling

blocks.note: copped is slang for caught or arrested

explanation.surface: A religious man in Egypt was arrested, it's said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collared' means nabbed by the police, which in slang is copped.
explanation.definitionFit: The Copts are Egypt's native Christians, members of the Coptic Orthodox Church, so a Copt is a believer.

clue.text: Seconder, being out of order, denied full expression

indicators.note: out of order means not in the proper sequence, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: At a meeting, a seconder speaking out of turn is cut off by the chair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of order' is the chairperson's ruling in the surface, and the rearrangement signal in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Censored material has had parts suppressed or cut, so it is not allowed to say everything.

clue.text: A biblical extract that’s intractable

blocks.note: a, as in 'a pound a head', means per
the Bible is divided into chapters and verses

explanation.surface: A difficult passage of scripture resists interpretation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' looks like the article but stands for per, as in 'ten pounds a day'.
explanation.definitionFit: Perverse describes someone stubbornly contrary, deliberately unreasonable and hard to manage or persuade.

clue.text: Harassed policemen losing months of time when mammals appeared

indicators.note: losing something means going without it, so a letter is dropped
harassed people are harried and disordered, so the letters are thrown about

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for months, the letter removed

explanation.surface: Stressed-out police officers lose track of months in the era when mammals arose.
explanation.walkthrough: Take M from POLICEMEN, then rearrange the remaining eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pliocene epoch, roughly five to two million years ago, saw many modern mammal groups emerge.

clue.text: Pour scorn on medicine, old vacuous remedy

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the inside is emptied out and only the outside letters stay

blocks.note: a pill is a dose of medicine
O is a standard abbreviation for old
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone mocks an outdated, useless cure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vacuous' reads as a scornful adjective for the remedy, but it empties the word to its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To pillory is to expose someone to public ridicule, as offenders once were in the stocks.

clue.text: Decorate lady’s cloak in orderly fashion

indicators.note: a cloak is the outer covering, so only the outside letters are kept

blocks.note: to trim a dress is to decorate it
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone neatly adorns a woman's cape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cloak' looks like a garment to decorate; it is the outer shell of the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Trimly means neatly and tidily, as something kept in good order and well arranged.

clue.text: Logical bloke, he’s one to be welcomed

indicators.note: someone welcomed is taken in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: cove is old British slang for a bloke or fellow
taken as written, without the apostrophe
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A reasonable man says he is the kind of guest people will welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He's one' is read literally as two pieces rather than as a description of the bloke; the apostrophe is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A cohesive argument hangs together well, its points connected consistently, which is what makes it logical.

clue.text: Token overthrow of rulers feasible

blocks.note: a coup is the sudden seizure of power from a government
something possible is on, as in 'that's not on'

explanation.surface: A merely symbolic toppling of the government is possible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Token' reads as an adjective meaning symbolic, but it is a noun: a voucher.
explanation.definitionFit: A coupon is a voucher exchanged for goods or a discount, which is the same thing as a token.

clue.text: Prepare insufficiently maybe for one style of bowling

blocks.note: first meaning, read as a made-up verb: to arm too little
second meaning: delivering the ball with the hand below the shoulder

explanation.walkthrough: The first half splits the word into UNDER plus ARM, a whimsical verb; 'maybe' admits that it is not a real one.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket and bowls a delivery with the hand kept below shoulder level is described by this word.

clue.text: Writer tries introducing current term of interest

indicators.note: to introduce something is to bring it in, so one piece is put inside another
a term is an end or limit, so only the final letter is taken

blocks.note: to essay is to attempt, so tries are essays
I is the physics symbol for electric current
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: An author attempts to bring in a fashionable word from the world of finance.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes into ESSAYS, then T is added. 'Term of interest' looks like a phrase from banking, but term means end.
explanation.definitionFit: An essayist is an author of short prose pieces, so is one kind of writer.

clue.text: Wife and I had to purchase device

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for wife
I'd is the contraction of I had
to get something can mean to buy it

explanation.surface: A couple needed to buy a new gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wife and I' reads as a couple, but 'and' just joins W to the contraction of 'I had'.
explanation.definitionFit: A widget is an informal name for a small gadget or mechanical contrivance, any unnamed device.
